questions.topic: C Basics — Purpose of the main Function
questions.q: What role does the main() function play in a C program?
questions.hint: Recall which function the compiler relies on when building a program to determine the starting point.
options: Serves as the entry point to the program, from whose body execution begins
Is an auxiliary module for loading system libraries
Is a mandatory preprocessor directive for code compression
Is called only when critical errors occur
explanations: Correct! The `main()` function is the main entry point of a C program. Execution of any C executable begins with the first instruction inside `main()`.
Incorrect. Header directives `#include` are responsible for including libraries.
Incorrect. `main()` is a C language function, not a preprocessor directive.
Incorrect. `main()` always executes upon program startup.

questions.q: What is the name of the executable file created by default by the GCC compiler when running gcc main.c in Linux?
questions.hint: Recall the historical default executable name preserved since early Unix systems.
options: a.out
main.exe
app.bin
output.o
explanations: Correct! If an output filename is not passed via the `-o` flag during compilation, GCC creates an executable named `a.out` (or `a.exe` on Windows OS).
Incorrect. By default, the name of the source `.c` file is not inherited by the binary file.
Incorrect. The name `app.bin` is not used by default.
Incorrect. Files with a `.o` extension are intermediate object files.

questions.q: What is the -o option used for when compiling a program with GCC?
questions.hint: Think about which parameter allows directing the compiler output into a target file with a custom name.
options: To specify a custom name for the created executable file
To enable maximum code optimization
To run the file in an interactive debugger
To save compilation logs to a file
explanations: Correct! The `-o filename` flag allows explicitly setting the compiled binary name instead of the default `a.out`.
Incorrect. Optimization is handled by flags in the `-O` family (e.g., `-O2`, `-O3`).
Incorrect. Debug information is generated using the `-g` flag.
Incorrect. The `-o` flag specifies the output binary filename.

questions.topic: C Basics — Address-of Operator & in scanf
questions.q: Why is the & operator placed before the variable name var when calling scanf("%d", &var)?
questions.hint: Think about what needs to be passed to an external function so it can directly update the variable's contents.
options: Passes the variable's memory address to scanf so the function can store the read value there
Automatically converts text to an integer
Indicates that variable var is global
Protects the variable from modification by other threads
explanations: Correct! The `&` operator returns the variable's memory address. `scanf` uses this address to store the user-entered value into the target memory cell.
Incorrect. Type conversion is performed by the format specifier `%d` itself.
Incorrect. The `&` operator does not affect variable scope.
Incorrect. The address-of operator is unrelated to thread synchronization.

questions.q: Which format specifier is used in printf to output float values?
questions.hint: Recall the specifier used to display floating-point (fractional) numbers in I/O functions.
options: %f
%d
%c
%s
explanations: Correct! Specifier `%f` is used for floating-point numbers (`float` or `double`), `%d` for integers (`int`), and `%c` for single characters (`char`).
Incorrect. `%d` outputs integers (`int`).
Incorrect. `%c` outputs single characters (`char`).
Incorrect. `%s` is used for string output.

questions.q: Which escape sequence in a C string literal moves the cursor to a new line?
questions.hint: Think of a special combination with a backslash used to format multi-line text output.
options: \n
\t
\b
explanations: Correct! The escape sequence `\n` performs a newline. `\t` handles tabbing, and `\b` handles backspacing.
Incorrect. `\t` inserts a tab character.
Incorrect. `\b` performs a backspace operation.
Incorrect. `\\` prints a single backslash character.

questions.topic: C Basics — Difference Between const and #define
questions.q: What is the main difference between declaring a constant const int N = 100 and a macro definition #define N 100?
questions.hint: Think about what happens to the code during preprocessor preprocessing and whether type rules are enforced.
options: const creates a typed constant with scope, while #define performs preprocessor text substitution
#define allows changing the value during program execution, while const does not
const is used only for floating-point numbers, while #define is used only for integers
The #define directive allocates RAM on the stack
explanations: Correct! The `#define` directive is processed by the preprocessor through plain text substitution prior to compilation. A `const` declaration creates a named variable with a fixed data type and scope rules.
Incorrect. Neither `const` nor `#define` constants can be modified at runtime.
Incorrect. Both approaches work with any data types.
Incorrect. `#define` does not allocate memory because the preprocessor merely substitutes text.

questions.topic: C Basics — Rules for Identifier Creation
questions.q: Which of the following variable names is INVALID according to C syntax rules?
questions.hint: Recall C syntax rules regarding the first character of an identifier.
options: 2count
_count2
count_2
CountTwo
explanations: Correct! An identifier in C must start with a letter or an underscore `_`. The name `2count` starts with a digit, which leads to a compilation error.
Incorrect. Starting a name with an underscore is permitted.
Incorrect. Using digits inside or at the end of a name is allowed.
Incorrect. Letters of any case are permitted.

questions.q: Are the identifiers myVar and MyVar identical from the C compiler's perspective?
questions.hint: Consider whether the C compiler distinguishes between uppercase and lowercase letters when searching for variable declarations.
options: No, C is case-sensitive, so these are two different identifiers
Yes, the compiler automatically converts all names to lowercase
Yes, if they are declared inside the same function
It depends on whether the GCC or Clang compiler is used
explanations: Correct! C is strictly case-sensitive: `myVar` and `MyVar` are treated by the compiler as completely distinct identifiers.
Incorrect. The compiler does not convert characters to a unified case.

questions.q: Which syntax is used for multi-line comments in C?
questions.hint: Pay attention to syntax constructs that enclose an entire block of text on both sides.
options: /* comment */
// comment //
<!-- comment -->
# comment
explanations: Correct! The `/* ... */` construct allows commenting out any block of text spanning multiple lines. Single-line comments use `//`.
Incorrect. `//` opens a single-line comment and does not require closing symbols.
Incorrect. `<!-- -->` is comment syntax in HTML/XML.
Incorrect. `#` is used for comments in Python/Bash or preprocessor directives in C.

questions.q: How does the C compiler interpret the statement x = x + 3;?
questions.hint: Distinguish between logical comparison and sequential expression evaluation followed by saving the result.
options: Evaluates the expression on the right (x + 3) and writes the result back into variable x
Checks algebraic equality and returns an error because x is not equal to x + 3
Causes an infinite loop due to self-reference
Replaces variable name x with value 3
explanations: Correct! The `=` operator first evaluates the right-hand side expression by adding 3 to the current value of `x`, then overwrites the result in variable `x`'s memory cell.
Incorrect. Assignment is distinct from mathematical equality. In C, equality checking uses the `==` operator.
Incorrect. This statement executes exactly once.
Incorrect. Variable name and memory structure remain unchanged.

questions.q: What does the % (modulo) operator calculate in C?
questions.hint: Think about what remains when one integer is divided by another with a remainder.
options: The remainder of integer division of the first operand by the second
The percentage ratio of the first number to the second
The quotient of division as a floating-point number
explanations: Correct! The `%` (modulus) operator returns the remainder of integer division. For example, `10 % 3` returns `1`.
Incorrect. The `%` operator is not related to calculating percentages.
Incorrect. The `/` operator is used to obtain the quotient.
